holdingBack: Pitch amplitude across the whole set: in the renderer headNod 1.0 is about 9 degrees (features slide 9 px, head group 5 px, scaleY 0.96), and every head action uses 0.2 to 0.6 of it, so nod, nodSlow, chinUp, lookUpThink and headBob are 2 to 5 px of feature slide on a 120 px head. Timing and ordering (eyes first, head second, shoulders third) are right in the keys and cannot be seen in the frames because nothing moves far enough.

The continuity cap caps realism, not just pops: headTurn 9.6/s and headNod 9.6/s (0.16 per frame) is about 145 deg/s of yaw, while a real 3 Hz shake at plus or minus 15 degrees peaks near 280 deg/s. velocity-shake.png already shows the plus or minus 0.35 shake in the red at 11/s, so the shake cannot be made real-sized under this test; either the cap for headTurn and headNod rises to about 20/s or the renderer gain (turn*16, nod*9) roughly doubles so the same channel values draw a real head. That is a REVIEW.md section 1 and src/rig/Face.tsx decision, outside head.ts.

Yaw and twist are translations, not rotations: in turnLeft frames 3 to 6 (0.45 to 0.90 s) the face slides 10 px across a skull and hair mass that stay put (skull 2.4 px, scaleX 0.97), and the 6 px twist slides the whole torso sideways off the hips, so the turn reads as the person shuffling left while her face slips across her head. The tilt sheets are the only ones that read as a rotating head, because headTilt is a real rotate; they also expose a hard slanted hair edge below the viewer-left ear at 10 to 12 degrees (tilt frames 2 to 5), which is an L1 draw matter.

findings.title: The head never follows the eyes: yaw is dead still for the whole sheet

findings.title: The weight shift is sub-pixel and the wrong shape: no counter-lean, no soft knee
findings.evidence: Code: src/rig/idle.ts lines 170-174 with stance = +-0.77 (seed 1, t 10-21 s) give bodyX contribution 1.15 px, upper-body translate 2.3 px via Body.tsx `stance * 3`, legs 1.2 px, lean 0.31 deg in the SAME direction as the translate, and kneeL/kneeR untouched. findings.real: When weight goes onto one foot the pelvis moves 2-4 cm out over that foot (1.5-2.5 % of height, 8-14 px here), the shoulder line tilts the opposite way so the head stays over the base (contrapposto), and the unweighted knee softens with the heel lifting slightly. Hip and shoulders moving the same way by 2 px is a lean, not a shift.

findings.title: The eyes glide back to centre over 250 ms: a smooth pursuit with nothing to pursue
findings.evidence: src/rig/idle.ts line 99: the return from the saccade target is `ease.inOut(clamp01((u - 0.06 - dwell) / 0.25))`. findings.real: Eyes have two speeds: a saccade (40-60 ms, ballistic) and smooth pursuit, which only happens when tracking a moving object. Returning the gaze to the viewer is another saccade, not a glide; a 250 ms eased slide of the iris is something a human eye cannot do without a target.

holdingBack: Arrival: every emotion fades in on one 0.35 s linear lerp with every channel in step, so a smile, a glare and a sob all land in the same frame and nothing leads; after 0.44 s every sheet is a frozen hold for 2 s.

The eyes do not participate: happy and grin keep neutral eyes (no Duchenne), surprised keeps neutral eyes under raised brows, angry keeps a bright open eye under a brow that crosses the lid, laugh closes the eye from the top instead of the bottom, thinking barely moves the gaze. Mouth and brows carry everything, which is what makes the hold read as a mask.

Mouth drawing conventions: the sad frown is a symmetric downward arc, the laugh teeth are a white band spanning the whole opening edge to edge, and the surprised O shows a flat dark floor; a photograph would have a straighter sad mouth with tucked corners, a narrower tooth arc with dark corners, and depth inside the O.

findings.title: Every expression arrives as one 0.35 s linear crossfade, all channels together, same speed for every emotion

holdingBack: The big arm actions (jumpJoy, stretch, celebrate on the way up) whip the shoulder at 1200 to 1850 deg/s straight from the wind-up with the elbow locked, so every one of them has a frame where the figure is a rigid horizontal T with the hands off-screen; nothing a camera could catch on a person.

The body-only actions are keyed at 1 to 4 percent of the figure (bow 13 px, leanIn 4 percent scale, leanBack 3 px shift, dance +-6 px, sway +-4 px, step with both feet planted), so eleven of the twelve sheets look like a still with the arms moving on it; the legs never separate and the hips never visibly shift weight.

findings.real: A smirk is one corner pulled up and back while the other stays flat or drops; a wink pulls the corner on the winking side up with the cheek. One-sided mouth movement is the entire signal of both gestures.
findings.where: mouthGeom, line 170 (`const cy = -pose.smile * 7`) and the path on line 173
findings.change: Give each corner its own lift derived from mouthX, the way smile physiology is derived here: `const cyL = -pose.smile * 7 * (1 - pose.mouthX * 2.4)` and `const cyR = -pose.smile * 7 * (1 + pose.mouthX * 2.4)`, then `M${-hw} ${cyL} C... ${hw} ${cyR} C... ${-hw} ${cyL} Z`; return cyL/cyR in MouthGeom and use them in the lower-lip body path (line 206) and the nasolabial crease endpoints (line 56). Smirk (smile 0.35, mouthX 0.25) then lifts the right corner 3.9 px and the left 1.0 px; neutral (mouthX 0.02) changes by 5 percent, which is nothing.

findings.title: The eyes cannot widen, so gasp and browRaise are brows only
findings.evidence: arjun-gesture-gasp.png frame 2 (0.20 s) and arjun-gesture-browRaise.png frame 3 (0.30 s): brows are 5 to 6 px up and pupils dilated, but the eye aperture is identical to frame 0; the iris still touches the upper lid. arjun-gesture-lookUp.png frame 4 (0.44 s): gaze up, brows up, lid unchanged.
findings.real: Surprise and a gasp lift the upper lid (AU5) and show white above the iris; that lid lift, not the brow, is what the eye catches first. Looking up also carries the upper lid up with the gaze.
findings.where: facePhysiology (lines 29 to 40) and Eye (line 113 `const c = -16 + ...` and the group transform on line 119)
findings.change: Derive a lid lift in facePhysiology: `const widen = clamp((pose.browL + pose.browR) / 2 - 0.3, 0, 0.6) + Math.max(0, -pose.lookY) * 0.15`; pass it to Eye and apply it as `scale(${sx} ${1 + widen * 0.3})` on the eye group so the almond (and its clip) grows taller, and `const c = -16 - widen * 6 + clamp(blink, 0, 1) * 27` so the upper lid control rises with it. Gasp (brows 0.85) then opens the eye 15 percent taller with white above the iris; neutral (brows 0.02) is untouched.

findings.title: Looking down shows white above the iris
findings.evidence: arjun-gesture-lookDown.png frame 4 (0.44 s) and frames 2 to 6: the iris sits at the bottom of the almond with a band of white above it, lids lowered only 22 percent (c = -10).
findings.real: When the gaze drops the upper lid follows the eyeball and covers the top third of the iris; sclera is never visible above the iris in a downward glance. It is what makes a lowered gaze read as lowered rather than as staring at the floor.
findings.where: Eye, line 113
findings.change: Make the upper lid follow a downward gaze in the renderer, so every action that looks down gets it: `const c = -16 + clamp(blink + Math.max(0, lookY) * 0.3, 0, 1) * 27`. lookDown (blink 0.22, lookY 0.9) then puts the lid control at -2.8, which covers the top of the iris (iris top at y = -3.6); sad (lookY 0.3) gets 9 percent heavier lids for free.

holdingBack: Every transit of a raised or folded forearm is planar: the arm windmills through a straight horizontal reach (raiseHand 1.42 s, countOne 0.28 s) or wipes across the belly (okSign 1.20 s, stopHand 1.27 s) because the rig cannot foreshorten the forearm toward the camera.

The held poses land in the wrong place on the body: stop and OK on the sternum (a pledge), the spread at the hips (akimbo), the beckon flat across the chest (a tray), the scratch hovering above the hair; the hold itself lives, but what it holds is not the gesture named.

At palm 1 the hand shapes collapse to mittens at slide size (fingerWag, the OK ring), so the meaning rides on the arm alone; the wind-ups are stiff straight-arm swings from the shoulder rather than an elbow cock.

findings.evidence: riya-gesture-raiseHand.png frame 9 (1.42 s): straight arm horizontal out to the side, hand clipped at the tile edge. riya-gesture-countOne.png frame 3 (0.28 s): forearm horizontal out at waist height, hand off the tile; frame 9 (1.14 s) and riya-gesture-countThree.png frame 10 (1.94 s): straight arm swung 30 deg out, hand dangling. riya-gesture-okSign.png frame 9 (1.20 s), riya-gesture-stopHand.png frame 9 (1.27 s), riya-gesture-rubHands.png frame 10 (1.76 s): forearm lying flat across the belly on the way down.

Nobody lowers a raised hand through a T-pose, and nobody drops a hand from the chest by wiping the forearm across the stomach. The rig has no out-of-plane rotation, so every elbow transit from a negative or large positive elbow to rest passes through a full-length horizontal forearm.
